title: US nuclear fusion tech advances as high-power gas lasers get DOE funds
excerpt: Fusion firm Xcimer Energy secured up to $30.5M in new DOE funding, utilizing innovative gas lasers and gas optics to target grid electricity.
content:
Commercial inertial nuclear fusion reactors require lasers that can fire high-energy pulses without wearing out. Xcimer Energy is developing an unconventional solution to this challenge. The company replaces solid-state glass optics with durable gases, aiming to supply electricity to the power grid by the mid-2030s.

This technical progress has qualified the firm for the second phase of the US Department of Energy’s Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program. The agreement unlocks up to $30.5m in performance-linked support. Unlike traditional research grants, these funds are released only after independent experts verify specific engineering benchmarks.

“Xcimer is making real progress toward a new generation of laser fusion technology, and this award will help accelerate that work,” said the DOE’s Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil.

Simple two-beamline layout

Most experimental laser fusion facilities rely on large banks of solid-state glass lasers. These systems split light into dozens or even hundreds of beams. While they can reach fusion conditions, solid-state lasers face severe hurdles inside a working power plant. The optical glass retains heat, takes hours to cool between shots, and cracks under continuous megajoule-scale bursts.

Xcimer’s architecture bypasses large solid-state laser glass. Instead, it uses excimer gas lasers paired with dynamic gas optics. Flowing gas mixtures act as both the laser medium and the focusing optics. Because the gas circulates constantly, it sheds waste heat quickly and cannot suffer permanent structural cracks.

This setup allows engineers to use a simple two-beamline layout instead of hundreds of delicate beam paths. The system is built to fire megajoule-class pulses at the steady repetition rates required for baseload electricity generation.

“We have moved from proving that the physics works to building the industrial technology that can turn fusion into a commercial energy source,” added Conner Galloway, co-founder and chief executive of Xcimer.

Testing platforms

The engineering roadmap centers on two primary platforms: Phoenix and Athena.

In June, the company commissioned Phoenix, the world’s largest privately owned laser system. Phoenix operates as a dedicated industrial test bed. It demonstrates that excimer gas lasers and gas optics can function reliably together at full scale.

Alongside work on Phoenix, the US Department of Energy completed an extensive review of Athena, Xcimer’s commercial power-plant architecture. The agency formally approved the preconceptual design and technology roadmap for the plant. Susana Reyes, vice-president of chamber design, noted that these formal reviews retire critical engineering risks before the team builds full-scale facilities.

Increasing demands of fusion power plant

The physical demands of a fusion power plant closely match those of directed-energy air defense. Both applications require a pulsed laser that fires rapid, high-energy shots at a low operating cost per joule.

Aerospace firm RTX has partnered with Xcimer to package this pulsed-laser hardware into compact, containerized units for military defense. Adapting the technology for mobile defense systems creates an immediate real-world testing ground. It also helps mature the industrial supply chains needed to deliver commercial fusion power.

“This additional milestone funding gives us another powerful mechanism to accelerate that work while keeping the majority of the investment and risk in the private sector,” concluded Galloway. “We are building the laser, manufacturing systems and supply chain required to make commercial laser fusion possible.”
